stem: Why should a magnesium ribbon be cleaned before burning in air?
solution:
Magnesium is a reactive metal. On standing in air its surface slowly reacts with oxygen and moisture and becomes coated with a dull layer of magnesium oxide. That coating is stable, and it keeps the metal underneath from catching fire readily.

Rubbing the ribbon with sandpaper strips the layer off and exposes clean magnesium, which then burns in air with a dazzling white flame to form magnesium oxide:

\(2\text{Mg}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{MgO}(s)\)
groundedIn: Activity 1.1 — 'Clean a magnesium ribbon about 3-4 cm long by rubbing it with sandpaper', then burn it; the reaction is the worked equation of §1.1.

context: Write the balanced equation for the following chemical reactions.
solution:
\(\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}(g)\)

One molecule each of hydrogen and chlorine gives two molecules of hydrogen chloride, so the coefficient 2 on the right is what balances the equation: 2 atoms of H and 2 of Cl on each side.

context: Write the balanced equation for the following chemical reactions.
stem: Barium chloride + Aluminium sulphate \(\rightarrow\) Barium sulphate + Aluminium chloride
solution:
\(3\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(aq) \rightarrow 3\text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{AlCl}_3(aq)\)

Count each element on both sides: Ba 3 and 3; Cl 6 and 6; Al 2 and 2; S 3 and 3; O 12 and 12. Balancing the sulphate and chloride groups as whole units is quicker than balancing S and O separately.

context: Write the balanced equation for the following chemical reactions.
solution:
\(2\text{Na}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Count each element on both sides: Na 2 and 2; O 2 and 2; H 4 and 4 — on the right, 2 hydrogen atoms sit in the two \(\text{OH}\) groups and 2 more in the \(\text{H}_2\) molecule.

context: Write a balanced chemical equation with state symbols for the following reactions.
stem: Solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate in water react to give insoluble barium sulphate and the solution of sodium chloride.
solution:
\(\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)\)

Both reactants are present as solutions in water, so each carries \((aq)\). Barium sulphate is insoluble and separates out as a white precipitate, so it carries \((s)\), while the sodium chloride stays dissolved and carries \((aq)\).
groundedIn: §1.1.2 introduces the notations (g), (l), (aq) and (s); this same reaction is carried out in Activity 1.10.

context: Write a balanced chemical equation with state symbols for the following reactions.
stem: Sodium hydroxide solution (in water) reacts with hydrochloric acid solution (in water) to produce sodium chloride solution and water.
solution:
\(\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

The equation is already balanced as written — Na 1 and 1, O 1 and 1, H 2 and 2, Cl 1 and 1. The water formed is a pure liquid, so it takes \((l)\) and not \((aq)\).

context: A solution of a substance 'X' is used for whitewashing.
stem: Name the substance 'X' and write its formula.
solution: 'X' is calcium oxide, commonly called quick lime. Its formula is \(\text{CaO}\).
groundedIn: §1.2.1 and Activity 1.4, where calcium oxide (quick lime) is reacted with water.

context: A solution of a substance 'X' is used for whitewashing.
stem: Write the reaction of the substance 'X' named in (i) above with water.
solution:
\(\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{Heat}\)

Calcium oxide reacts vigorously with water to give calcium hydroxide (slaked lime), releasing a large amount of heat. Two reactants combine to give a single product, so this is a combination reaction. It is the slaked lime formed here that is used for whitewashing.

stem: Why is the amount of gas collected in one of the test tubes in Activity 1.7 double of the amount collected in the other? Name this gas.
solution:
Activity 1.7 is the electrolysis of water, in which water is decomposed by passing electricity through it:

\(2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \xrightarrow{\text{Electricity}} 2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)\)

A water molecule contains two atoms of hydrogen for every one atom of oxygen, so decomposing it releases hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1 by volume. The test tube that collects twice as much gas is therefore the one over the cathode, and the gas in it is **hydrogen**.
groundedIn: Activity 1.7 and Fig. 1.6 (electrolysis of water), in §1.2.2.

stem: Why does the colour of copper sulphate solution change when an iron nail is dipped in it?
solution:
Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution:

\(\text{Fe}(s) + \text{CuSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

The blue colour of the original solution comes from copper sulphate. As the reaction proceeds the copper sulphate is used up and iron sulphate takes its place, and iron sulphate solution is green — so the blue fades to green. The copper that has been displaced deposits on the nail as a reddish-brown coating.
groundedIn: Activity 1.9 (iron nails in copper sulphate solution) and §1.2.3.

stem: Give an example of a double displacement reaction other than the one given in Activity 1.10.
solution:
Sodium chloride solution reacting with silver nitrate solution:

\(\text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{AgNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s) + \text{NaNO}_3(aq)\)

The two reactants exchange ions — chloride moves to silver and nitrate to sodium. Silver chloride is insoluble and comes down as a white precipitate, so this is a precipitation reaction as well as a double displacement reaction.
groundedIn: §1.2.4 defines double displacement as an exchange of ions; Activity 1.10 is the example the question excludes.

context: Identify the substances that are oxidised and the substances that are reduced in the following reactions.
solution:
**Sodium is oxidised** — it gains oxygen to become sodium oxide.

**Oxygen is reduced** — it is the species that combines with sodium, and in the oxygen-transfer picture the substance supplying oxygen to another is itself reduced.
groundedIn: §1.2.5 — 'if a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen during a reaction, it is oxidised. If a substance loses oxygen or gains hydrogen during a reaction, it is reduced.'

context: Identify the substances that are oxidised and the substances that are reduced in the following reactions.
solution:
**Copper oxide is reduced** — it loses oxygen and is left as copper metal.

**Hydrogen is oxidised** — it gains oxygen and becomes water.

Both changes happen in the same reaction, so this is a redox reaction.
groundedIn: §1.2.5 — 'if a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen during a reaction, it is oxidised. If a substance loses oxygen or gains hydrogen during a reaction, it is reduced.'
